evidence.description: The instance stores the task, which promotes its weak capture to a strong reference before entering the repeating loop.
The only visible cancellation is performed during deinitialization.

candidates.explanation: Although the task initially captures self weakly, the guard creates a strong reference that remains alive throughout the repeating loop, including its suspension points. The instance retains the task, and cancellation occurs only in deinit. Consequently, releasing other references cannot trigger the deinitializer that would stop the task.
candidates.title: Timer task retains its owner indefinitely

evidence.description: The interval is multiplied and converted directly to UInt64.
The reciprocal calculation has no zero-rate or finite-value handling.
The date-based floating-point projection is converted directly to Int.

candidates.explanation: The timer interval calculation does not handle a zero investment rate: division produces infinity, which passes through max and cannot be converted to UInt64 for sleeping. The projected investment total is likewise converted to Int without checking that it is finite and representable. These conversions can terminate execution rather than produce a valid result when their inputs exceed the integer domains.
candidates.title: Unchecked floating-point conversions can trap

evidence.description: The initial interval is assigned to an unused local constant.
The loop independently retrieves the interval that is actually used for sleeping.

candidates.explanation: The task awaits an initial interval and stores it in initialInterval, but never reads that value. The loop fetches another interval before sleeping, making the initial asynchronous read redundant and adding an unnecessary suspension point before the first update.
candidates.title: Initial timer interval is fetched but never used
